extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate_and_graduate_philosophy_students; scholars of Kant; readers studying teleology and the Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Kant's principles and maxims for judging purposiveness in nature (teleology) as presented in the Critique of Judgment, including distinctions between reflective and determinant judgement and accounts of systems (idealism/realism) about purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural purpose as regulative, not constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: “The concept of a thing as in itself a natural purpose is therefore no constitutive concept of Understanding or of Reason, but it can serve as a regulative concept for the reflective Judgement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the idea of natural purpose only as a regulative principle to guide reflective investigation (analogy to our own causality), not as a constitutive principle that supplies objective knowledge of nature's causes. Do not treat natural-purpose-talk as providing new causal facts about nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of organised product (internal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “An organised product of nature is one in which every part is reciprocally purpose, and means. In it nothing is vain, without purpose, or to be ascribed to a blind mechanism of nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a natural thing as organised when its parts stand in reciprocal end/means relations; this furnishes objective reality to the concept 'purpose of nature' and grounds teleological investigation of such objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: nothing in organised beings is vain; teleological maxim for observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissectors and investigators assume as a maxim that nothing in such a creature is 'vain' and that 'nothing happens by chance.' This is derived from observation but requires an a priori principle (a maxim) for the reflective judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a necessary regulative maxim to guide systematic observation of organisms; it is not an empirical theorem but a reflective rule that legitimates teleological inquiry into internal form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: internal vs external purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: External purposiveness (relations of things to our uses) does not warrant taking them as purposes of nature; internal form (organisation) is what gives grounds to judge something as a natural purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count externally useful relations (e.g., rivers useful to humans) as evidence that a thing is a natural purpose. Only internal purposive organisation justifies teleological judgment about a thing's possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging internal purposiveness ≠ asserting final purpose of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a thing as a natural purpose on account of its internal form is different from taking the existence of that thing to be a purpose of nature; the latter requires knowledge of the final purpose (scopus) of nature and reference to the supersensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit teleological claims: internal purposiveness supports a merely reflective judgement about possibilities, not a substantive metaphysical claim that the thing exists for a final, world-encompassing purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulative principle of collective nature as system of purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of natural purposes leads to the Idea of collective nature as a system in accordance with the rule of purposes; a maxim of Reason: 'everything in the World is some way good for something; nothing is vain in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ this as a subjective, regulative maxim to guide the extension of natural science toward seeing nature as a purposive system, while recognizing it has no constitutive authority to establish metaphysical ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology as a mode of judging, not a substitute for mechanical causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological judgement is regulative and supplementary: it gives a different kind of investigation from mechanical causality but does not prejudice or replace mechanical explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological explanations only to supplement and guide inquiry where mechanical explanations are inadequate; always keep teleological reflection open to mechanical accounts and avoid treating teleology as an independent causal theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not introduce theological (foreign) principles as domestic to natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences that borrow concepts from outside (foreign principles) place auxiliary propositions at their basis. Introducing the concept of God into natural science as an internal principle results in circularity and delusive mixing of boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural science must avoid treating theological concepts as internal principles; teleological discourse should be couched as a methodological analogue (purpose-talk about nature) rather than a theological explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori natural characteristics are not teleological grounds for Physics
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural characteristics that demonstrate themselves a priori (arithmetical/geometrical analogies, universal mechanical laws) cannot be referred to the Teleology of nature as internal principles of Physic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake mathematical or a priori regularities for teleological explanations within physics; such analogies belong to metaphysics and cannot serve as internal teleological principles for empirical natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak of nature's 'wisdom' or 'economy' only analogically for reflective use
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to speak of the wisdom, economy, forethought, beneficence of Nature in Teleology, but only as an analogy for the reflective (not determinant) Judgement and without ascribing actual intelligent design to inanimate matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological language as heuristic analogy to guide investigation, making explicit that such language is not literal attribution of intelligence or a supernatural architect; avoid slipping into metaphysical or theological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: First maxim (mechanical) of reflective judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: First maxim of Judgement: all production of material things and their forms must be judged to be possible according to merely mechanical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a regulative rule, always attempt mechanical explanations first; reflective judgement must use mechanical principles as the first guiding maxim for investigating natural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second maxim (teleological) of reflective judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Second maxim (counter-proposition): some products of material nature cannot be judged to be possible according to merely mechanical laws; to judge them requires a different law of causality, namely that of final causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit teleological reflection where mechanical inquiry cannot furnish the least ground for specific purposive characters; treat this as a secondary regulative maxim, not a constitutive principle asserting real, distinct causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid converting regulative maxims into constitutive principles (solution to antinomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent antinomy between mechanical and teleological maxims arises from confusing regulative (reflective) propositions with constitutive (determinant) principles; we cannot prove either objective proposition a priori, so we must keep them as maxims for reflective judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve conflicts by maintaining the autonomy of the reflective judgement and its maxims; do not assert as unprovable objective truths what serve only as methodological guides for inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two explanatory systems: Idealism vs Realism of natural purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems about Technic (purposive production) of nature divide into Idealism (purposiveness is undesigned—casuality or fatality) and Realism (some purposiveness is designed—either hylozoism or theism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating accounts of teleology, classify them as idealist (explaining purposiveness as emergent/accidental or necessary) or realist (ascribing design or life to matter or positing an intelligent ground), and be aware each leads to different metaphysical commitments and problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical requirement: explanatory account must secure unity of purpose without destroying contingency
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Spinoza and Epicurus: a satisfactory system must make purposive connection intelligible in virtue of a cause with Understanding (design) or else cannot account for unity of purpose; conversely, denying contingency (as Spinoza does) undermines design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess teleological theories by whether they explain purposive unity in a way that preserves contingency and intelligible purposive reference; systems that either reduce purposiveness to blind chance or eliminate contingency fail to explain teleological judgment.
